progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: chem-m5-c13 (NAGSAG, net ionic equations, spectators; AgCl white, PbI₂ bright yellow, BaSO₄ white, Cu(OH)₂ pale blue); chem-m5-c14 and chem-m5-c15 (a solid forms once the ion product passes Ksp; "slightly soluble" is a recall word only); Module 5 equilibrium (FeSCN²⁺ blood red); Year 11 Module 1 (flame tests, emission). Oxidation of Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺ is named in plain words (loses an electron to oxygen), not taught.
progression.startsWith: Use flame colour and precipitate evidence. The video opens: A prep room shelf holds eight bottles of solutions, and the labels have washed off. Each one holds a different metal ion: barium, calcium, magnesium, lead, silver, copper, and iron in two forms, iron two and iron three. A sample from one bottle is in this tube.
progression.stopsAfter: naming the three kinds of evidence; running the chloride, sulfate and hydroxide steps in order with the reason for the order; splitting Ag⁺ from Pb²⁺, Ba²⁺ from Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ from Ca²⁺; reading the four hydroxide colours and the Fe²⁺ trap; confirming with complexes; drawing the cation flowchart; writing the net ionic equation for the deciding precipitate. No anions, no procedure or risk table.
progression.nextLesson: identifying the anion (route chem-m8-c03b), then the practical with unknowns (chem-m8-p03).

teaching.task: Eight bottles on a prep room shelf have lost their labels. Each holds a different metal ion. How can a short sequence of tests, each ruling ions out, tell you which metal ion is in a sample, and how do you confirm it?
teaching.causalExplanation: (1) one test won't settle eight suspects; a sequence of tests rules ions out; (2) a precipitate test adds an anion that makes an insoluble solid with only some cations (solubility rules recall); a flame test reads the light given out by the heated sample's atoms; a complex ion is a metal ion with molecules or ions bonded around it, often coloured or able to pull a solid back into solution; (3) chloride: only silver and lead chlorides are insoluble, so white means Ag⁺ or Pb²⁺, and no solid rules both out (but dilute lead may slip through); (4) ammonia bonds to silver ions, so AgCl dissolves and PbCl₂ doesn't; KI gives bright yellow PbI₂; (5) sulfate: BaSO₄ insoluble; CaSO₄ slightly soluble, so only concentrated calcium shows; PbSO₄ catches dilute lead; a white solid here needs one more test; (6) flame colour: heat excites electrons in the sample's atoms, they fall back and emit light characteristic of the element; Ba²⁺ pale green, Ca²⁺ brick red, Cu²⁺ blue-green, Mg²⁺ and Pb²⁺ no useful colour; (7) flame limits: sodium masks, dirty loop carries over, so clean it and back each flame with a precipitate; (8) hydroxide: four coloured solids; Mg(OH)₂ white and stays in excess; a white solid could be concentrated Ca²⁺, so a colourless flame points to Mg²⁺; (9) why chloride and sulfate come first: Ag⁺ and Pb²⁺ would also give hydroxide solids; (10) Fe(OH)₂ browns in air as Fe²⁺ is oxidised to Fe³⁺, so read it at once; (11) complexes confirm: Cu²⁺ with excess ammonia, deep blue; Fe³⁺ with thiocyanate, blood red; two kinds of chemistry agreeing is stronger evidence; (12) the flowchart and the hook sample traced; the chart is for one unknown cation, and mixtures need a separation plan.
teaching.conversationalApproach: eight bottles on a prep room shelf have lost their labels, each holding a different metal ion, and a blue tint only hints at copper, so the video asks how a short sequence of tests can rule ions out until one is left and then confirm it. Three kinds of evidence are introduced: a precipitate test adds an anion that makes an insoluble solid with only some cations, a flame test reads the colour of the heated sample, and a complexation test bonds molecules or ions around the metal ion. The plan is to sort with precipitates, each in a fresh portion: dilute hydrochloric acid first, where a white solid means silver or lead, split by dilute ammonia dissolving silver chloride and by potassium iodide giving yellow lead iodide, with dilute lead able to slip through; then dilute sulfuric acid, where barium and concentrated calcium give white sulfates; then the flame test as supporting evidence (pale green barium, brick red calcium, blue-green copper), with its limits from sodium and a dirty loop. Sodium hydroxide comes third, giving pale blue copper, red-brown iron(III), green iron(II) and white magnesium hydroxides, and the order matters because silver and lead would muddy those colours. The iron(II) trap is that air oxidises the green solid to brown, so read it at once. Complexes confirm: excess ammonia gives deep blue with copper and thiocyanate gives blood red with iron(III). The flowchart traces the hook sample to copper. The memory aid is chloride, sulfate, hydroxide, then flame, with the ions each step catches. Two exam questions follow with brief feedback.
teaching.openingDecision: A prep room shelf holds eight bottles of solutions, and the labels have washed off. Each one holds a different metal ion: barium, calcium, magnesium, lead, silver, copper, and iron in two forms, iron two and iron three. A sample from one bottle is in this tube. A blue tint might hint at copper, but a hint isn't proof. One test won't settle eight suspects. We need a sequence of tests, where each result rules some ions out.
teaching.understandingCheck: (A1) Separate portions: dilute HCl no change; dilute H₂SO₄ white precipitate; pale green flame. Identify the cation and write the net ionic equation. Tests the sequence logic and the flame as decider. Crossed mistake: "Ca²⁺: it gave a white sulfate" (pack trap: "flame colour treated as unique proof" turned round; site MC idea, original wording). (A2) Green NaOH precipitate turns red-brown after ten minutes; student concludes Fe³⁺. Evaluate and suggest a confirming test. Tests scene 10's cause. Crossed mistake: "Fe³⁺: the final colour is red-brown".
teaching.curriculumScope: Syllabus (NSW Chemistry Stage 6, 2017), as printed: "conduct qualitative investigations – using flame tests, precipitation and complexation reactions as appropriate – to test for the presence in aqueous solution of the following ions:; cations: barium (Ba2+), calcium (Ca2+), magnesium (Mg2+), lead(II) (Pb2+), silver ion (Ag+), copper(II) (Cu2+), iron(II) (Fe2+), iron(III) (Fe3+); anions: chloride (Cl–), bromide (Br–), iodide (I–), hydroxide (OH–), acetate (CH3COO–), carbonate (CO32–), sulfate (SO42–), phosphate (PO43–)" (The two dashes in the first line are en dashes as printed, not em dashes.) This video covers the eight cations. The anions are chem-m8-c03b; the hands-on investigation with unknowns is chem-m8-p03. starts from a sample holding one unknown metal ion from the syllabus list, and stops when the student can sort and confirm it with a test sequence and write the net ionic equation for the deciding precipitate. It teaches: three kinds of evidence (precipitate, flame, complex) with a plain meaning each; a fresh portion for each test; step 1, dilute HCl: white AgCl or PbCl₂ (Ag⁺, Pb²⁺); the split by dilute ammonia (AgCl dissolves as [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺) and by KI (bright yellow PbI₂); step 2, dilute H₂SO₄: white BaSO₄ (Ba²⁺), CaSO₄ only from fairly concentrated samples, PbSO₄ for lead that slipped through; flame tests (Ba²⁺ pale green, Ca²⁺ brick red, Cu²⁺ blue-green; Mg²⁺ and Pb²⁺ no useful colour), with the cause in one recall sentence and the sodium and dirty-loop limits; step 3, NaOH: Cu(OH)₂ pale blue, Fe(OH)₂ green, Fe(OH)₃ red-brown, Mg(OH)₂ white (stays in excess); why the chloride and sulfate steps come first; Fe(OH)₂ browning in air; complex confirmations (Cu²⁺ with excess NH₃ deep blue; Fe³⁺ with SCN⁻ blood red); the full flowchart, with its two branch conditions kept; one sentence that mixtures need a separation plan (not taught here). Not taught: anions (c03b); Al³⁺, NH₄⁺, Na⁺, K⁺, Li⁺, Sr²⁺ (site extension, not syllabus); amphoteric Pb(OH)₂ and Ag₂O with hydroxide beyond one clause; hexacyanoferrate tests for iron; AAS (c04); the procedure and risk table (p03).

design.visualSystem: Explainer engine: warm paper stage, handwritten Caveat headings, amber doodle layer. Colour key: chloride step green; sulfate step amber; hydroxide step blue; flame step orange; complex step violet; precipitates in their real colours; the current box bright; completed families dim grey. Board layout (constant): suspect strip along the top; heading below it top-left; tube or flame plates left third; flowchart right two thirds, growing downward. Reuse: painted plates inspected 30 Oct by contact sheet (Assets). The m5x rack set and the m8 rack plates are different racks, so only m5x-rack tubes appear side by side; the brief 60 `m8-ppt-feoh2-green-v1.png` (m8 rack) is not used, and a matching m5x-rack retake is requested. No human figures.
design.transitionPlan: The heading writes on over eight blank-label bottles as the suspect strip writes one symbol per ion; three small evidence panels write left to right, the complex wrap inset clustering ammonia around a cation; the board clears to the flowchart area, where each reagent arrow writes down from the sample box, a reagent drop falls into the rack tube and the tube cross-fades to its precipitate state with the net ionic equation beside it; the ammonia split runs in the complex wrap inset as the silver chloride tile breaks up; the unlit burner plate gives way to each flame plate on its cue, then the sodium glow spreads over the green; the four hydroxide tubes write in a row in the aligned rack; ghost tiles for silver and lead drop and strike out as the suspect strip narrows; the green iron(II) tube enlarges and cross-fades to its browning plate under a clock arc; violet confirmation arrows write under the copper and iron(III) boxes with the deep blue and blood red tubes; the full flowchart lights family by family and a highlight traces the hook sample to copper; the memory lines write with colour swatches; each attempt clears the board with its question card, and its feedback underlines the card as the mini flowchart path lights and a crossed trap chip lands; the hook bottle returns with a next chip; scene crossfade with settle.
